name: Consortium Blockchain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Consortium Blockchains: Trust Shared Among a Chosen Few
lesson.summary: A consortium blockchain is a permissioned network jointly governed by a pre-selected group of organizations, sitting between a single-company private blockchain and a fully open public network.
lesson.body:
A consortium blockchain is a permissioned blockchain governed jointly by a pre-selected group of organizations rather than by one company alone or by the open public. It sits deliberately between the two models covered in the last two chapters: more distributed than a private blockchain, where a single organization controls everything, but far more restricted than a permissionless public network, where anyone can join without a vote.

The clearest way to picture this is a group of banks that need a shared ledger for something like interbank settlement or trade finance, where several institutions are recording the same underlying transactions and need to agree on a single version of events. No individual bank wants a rival institution to unilaterally control the shared system, and none of them want the general public running validating nodes on infrastructure that touches real financial settlement. A consortium arrangement lets each participating bank run its own validating node, so that reaching consensus requires genuine agreement among multiple independent institutions, none of which can simply overrule the others the way a single controlling company could in a private blockchain.

The governance mechanics matter as much as the technology here. A consortium typically operates under an explicit charter or agreement, negotiated in advance, that spells out who counts as a member, how new members are added or removed, how validator nodes are assigned, and how disputes or proposed protocol changes get decided, often through some form of voting among the member organizations. This is a meaningful contrast with a permissionless network, where joining requires no vote or agreement from anyone, and with a private blockchain, where one company simply decides the rules by itself without needing anyone else's consent.

Positioned this way, a consortium blockchain is a practical answer to a specific kind of trust problem: several organizations that each have some reason not to fully trust the others, but that still need a shared, tamper evident record they can all rely on without appointing one of themselves as the sole administrator. It is not a compromise chosen out of indecision so much as a direct match to situations where the parties involved are known to each other, have real legal relationships, and need coordination more than they need openness to strangers.

Financial institutions have been among the most visible adopters of this model, with platforms such as R3's Corda built specifically around a small set of known, permissioned participants transacting with each other, illustrating the consortium pattern in practice. The next chapter looks at Hyperledger, an open source family of tools that many organizations, including consortiums like this, actually build these permissioned and private networks on top of.
